title: Kidnapped Simulator
author: Content-Building-405
selftext:
**What we learned building a horror game around one offline AI character**

We've been working on **Kidnapped Simulator**, and we're finally sharing its first trailer. It's a psychological horror game set in one room, where you type your own replies to your captor, Abel Marsh. Since this is r/aigamedev, I wanted to share a little of the development behind it.

One question has shaped a lot of our work: how do you make a generated conversation feel like it belongs to someone physically present in the room?

Abel's dialogue comes from a local language model through our custom conversation system. Speech generation also runs on the player's PC. The game works offline, and the conversation stays on the machine. Underneath that, we still have authored story structure, game state, events, and prepared animations. Giving the player an open text field means allowing unexpected answers while keeping the character and the situation coherent.

A surprising amount of iteration has been about hands, posture, and objects. A character can deliver a convincing line and immediately lose you by holding a book with an impossible wrist angle. We went through repeated passes on how Abel carries his ledger, sits down, handles small objects, and looks at the player. Fixing a hand in isolation often made the rest of the movement look worse. The shoulder, torso, timing, and object contact all had to agree. That became a useful lesson for the whole project: judge the complete interaction, not just the output of each system.

The visual direction changed too. We initially leaned closer to PS2-era horror, then moved towards a rougher PS1-inspired look after feedback. AI-assisted visual exploration helped us test that direction, but getting it into the game still required work on the models, textures, lighting, and framing. Adding more pixelation alone didn't get us there.

Running everything locally also gives us a shared hardware budget for the game, dialogue, and voice. For us, waiting time is part of the scene's pacing, so evaluating the conversation system means watching and listening to the encounter as well as reading the replies.

We're still developing it, but this trailer is our first proper introduction to the world we've been building. I'd be interested to hear from others working on AI characters: **which part has taken the most iteration for you once the dialogue was working?**

If you'd like to follow the project, here's our [Steam page.](https://store.steampowered.com/app/4550740/Kidnapped_Simulator/)

replies.author: Crunchfest3
replies.body: Which part interests you the most? When it comes to the kidnapper character, knowledge of how to build AI models is key, because we’re training our own model from scratch here, so understanding transformers, datasets, etc., is what matters.

How do you keep the LLM ‘making sense’ and responding logically? Looks like a slam dunk game! Thank you!

comments.author: UpDown
comments.body: The AI disclosure on steam is weird to me. What does 'selected character and environment textures" even mean? I assume if youre using AI for at youre using 100%, so why say selected? How much was selected? "*I tools were also used during development to create and edit selected character and environment textures and other visual assets included in the game."*

replies.author: Crunchfest3
replies.body: Well, it would be hard to specify which asset was modified and to what extent—the art style is “human”; some assets were purchased off-the-shelf, some were modified using AI, and some were created from scratch, which is why I described it that way. Overall, the art style isn't typically AI-generated; here, AI was used to speed up the art production process.
